title: Assignment 1 - Brush up R and Quarto
text:
Introduction
This assignment reviews basic R programming, Quarto formatting, and exploratory data analysis using the TEDS 2016 dataset. The purpose is to become familiar with data structures in R, identify potential data problems, handle missing values, and explore possible relationships between political attitude variables.
Load Required Packages
{r} # Install packages if needed # install.packages(c(“tidyverse”, “haven”, “skimr”, “janitor”))
library(tidyverse) library(haven) library(skimr) library(janitor)
Load the Dataset
{r} TEDS_2016 <- haven::read_dta( “https://github.com/datageneration/home/blob/master/DataProgramming/data/TEDS_2016.dta?raw=true” )
Explore the Dataset
Display the Dataset
{r} head(TEDS_2016)
View Dataset Structure
{r} glimpse(TEDS_2016)
Summary Statistics
{r} summary(TEDS_2016)
Check Variable Names
{r} names(TEDS_2016)
Exploratory Data Analysis
Missing Values
{r} missing_values <- colSums(is.na(TEDS_2016)) missing_values |> sort(decreasing = TRUE) |> head(15)
Overall Dataset Summary
{r} skim(TEDS_2016)
Problems Encountered in the Dataset
Several problems were identified while working with the TEDS 2016 dataset.

Missing Values

Many variables contain missing observations. Missing values can reduce sample size and affect statistical accuracy.

Labelled Variables

Some variables are imported as labelled variables instead of numeric or factor variables. This can create problems when running statistical models.

Difficult Variable Names

Some variable names are abbreviated and difficult to understand without documentation.

Uneven Categories

Certain categorical variables contain categories with very few observations.

Data Cleaning Requirements

Some variables require recoding before analysis.
Handling Missing Values
There are several approaches for handling missing values.
Remove Missing Values
{r} TEDS_clean <- na.omit(TEDS_2016)
Replace Missing Values
Example using mean replacement:
{r} TEDS_2016\(age[is.na(TEDS_2016\)age)] <- mean( TEDS_2016$age, na.rm = TRUE )
Why Missing Values Matter
Missing data can:
Reduce statistical power
Create biased results
Affect regression models
Reduce prediction accuracy
Therefore, careful data cleaning is important before conducting analysis.
Relationship Between Tondu and Other Variables
The assignment asks us to explore the relationship between Tondu and other variables including:
female
DPP
age
income
edu
Taiwanese
Econ_worse
Several statistical methods can be used.
Possible Statistical Methods

Frequency Tables

Frequency tables help summarize distributions of categorical variables.

Cross-Tabulation

Cross-tabulation can compare relationships between two categorical variables.
Example:
{r} # Example cross-tabulation # table(TEDS_2016\(Tondu, TEDS_2016\)female)

Correlation Analysis

Correlation can examine relationships between numeric variables.

Regression Analysis

Linear regression or logistic regression can estimate relationships between dependent and independent variables.
Example:
{r} model1 <- lm(age ~ income + edu, data = TEDS_2016) summary(model1)

Visualization

Graphs can help identify patterns and trends.
Exploring the votetsai Variable
The variable votetsai represents voting behavior related to Tsai Ing-wen.
Possible analyses include:
Frequency analysis
Cross-tabulation with party identification
Logistic regression
Classification models
Frequency Table for votetsai
{r} table(TEDS_2016$votetsai)
Recode Tondu Variable
The assignment requests assigning labels to the Tondu variable.
{r} TEDS_2016\(Tondu <- factor(
  as.numeric(TEDS_2016\)Tondu), labels = c( “Unification now”, “Status quo, unif. in future”, “Status quo, decide later”, “Status quo forever”, “Status quo, indep. in future”, “Independence now”, “No response” ) )
Frequency Table of Tondu
{r} table(TEDS_2016$Tondu)
Bar Chart of Tondu
{r} ggplot(TEDS_2016, aes(x = Tondu)) + geom_bar() + theme_minimal() + labs( title = “Distribution of Tondu”, x = “Tondu Category”, y = “Frequency” ) + theme( axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1) )
Interpretation of Results
The bar chart shows the distribution of political attitudes regarding Taiwanese independence and unification. Some categories appear much more frequently than others, suggesting that public opinion is concentrated in several major political positions.
The exploratory analysis also demonstrates that political attitudes may be associated with demographic characteristics such as age, education, and party preference.
Conclusion
This assignment reviewed basic R programming and Quarto usage while conducting exploratory data analysis using the TEDS 2016 dataset. Several challenges were identified, including missing values, labelled variables, and categorical data issues. Different statistical methods such as cross-tabulation, regression, and visualization can be used to further analyze relationships between political variables.
Overall, this assignment provided useful experience in data cleaning, exploratory analysis, and political data interpretation using R.
References
Wickham, H., Çetinkaya-Rundel, M., & Grolemund, G. R for Data Science
TEDS 2016 Dataset
EPPS6323 Knowledge Mining Course Materials

title: Assignment 4 - Text Analytics using quanteda
text:
This assignment applies text analytics methods using the quanteda package in R. The purpose is to analyze political text data, identify similarities and differences across documents, and apply scaling techniques such as Wordfish to compare document positions.
Text analytics is increasingly important in political science, social science, and machine learning because it allows researchers to study large collections of documents systematically.

title: Assignment 4 - Text Analytics using quanteda
text:
11.1 Similarities
Several themes consistently appear across presidential inaugural speeches.
Common themes include:

Democracy
Freedom
National unity
Economic prosperity
American values

These themes reflect the traditional goals of presidential speeches.

title: Assignment 4 - Text Analytics using quanteda
text:
11.2 Differences
Important differences can also be observed across presidents and historical periods.

11.2.1 Earlier Presidents
Earlier speeches often focused on:

Nation building
Constitutional principles
Territorial expansion



11.2.2 War-Time Presidents
War-time speeches emphasized:

Military strength
National security
Patriotism



11.2.3 Modern Presidents
Modern speeches discuss:

Globalization
Technology
Climate change
Diversity
International cooperation

Political ideology also affects speech content and language choices.

title: EPPS 6323: Lab02 R programming basics II
text:
R Programming Basic Commands
(Adapted from ISLR Chapter 3 Lab: Introduction to R)
Indexing Data using []
{r} A=matrix(1:16,4,4) A A[2,3] A[c(1,3),c(2,4)] A[1:3,2:4] A[1:2,] A[,1:2] A[1,] A[-c(1,3),] # What does -c() do? A[-c(1,3),-c(1,3,4)] dim(A) # Dimensions
Loading Data from GitHub (remote)
{r} Auto=read.table(“https://raw.githubusercontent.com/datageneration/knowledgemining/master/data/Auto.data”) Auto=read.table(“https://raw.githubusercontent.com/datageneration/knowledgemining/master/data/Auto.data”,header=T,na.strings=“?”) Auto=read.csv(“https://raw.githubusercontent.com/datageneration/knowledgemining/master/data/Auto.csv”) # read csv file # Which function reads data faster?

Try using this simple method


time1 = proc.time()


Auto=read.csv(“https://raw.githubusercontent.com/datageneration/knowledgemining/master/data/Auto.csv”,header=T,na.strings=“?”)


proc.time()-time1


Check on data
dim(Auto) Auto[1:4,] # select rows Auto=na.omit(Auto) dim(Auto) # Notice the difference? names(Auto)
Load data from ISLR website
{r Loaddata_from_web} Auto=read.table(“https://www.statlearning.com/s/Auto.data”,header=T,na.strings=“?”) dim(Auto)
Additional Graphical and Numerical Summaries
{r} # plot(cylinders, mpg) plot(Auto\(cylinders, Auto\)mpg) attach(Auto) plot(cylinders, mpg) cylinders=as.factor(cylinders) plot(cylinders, mpg) plot(cylinders, mpg, col=“red”) plot(cylinders, mpg, col=“red”, varwidth=T) plot(cylinders, mpg, col=“red”, varwidth=T,horizontal=T) plot(cylinders, mpg, col=“red”, varwidth=T, xlab=“cylinders”, ylab=“MPG”) hist(mpg) hist(mpg,col=2) hist(mpg,col=2,breaks=15) #pairs(Auto) pairs(~ mpg + displacement + horsepower + weight + acceleration, Auto) plot(horsepower,mpg) # identify(horsepower,mpg,name) # Interactive: point and click the dot to identify cases summary(Auto) summary(mpg)
Linear Regression
{r} ptbu=c(“MASS”,“ISLR”) install.packages(ptbu, repos=‘http://cran.us.r-project.org’) lapply(ptbu, require, character.only = TRUE) library(MASS) library(ISLR)


Simple Linear Regression


fix(Boston)
names(Boston) # lm.fit=lm(medv~lstat) attach(Boston) lm.fit=lm(medv~lstat,data=Boston) attach(Boston) lm.fit=lm(medv~lstat) lm.fit summary(lm.fit) names(lm.fit) coef(lm.fit) confint(lm.fit) predict(lm.fit,data.frame(lstat=(c(5,10,15))), interval=“confidence”) predict(lm.fit,data.frame(lstat=(c(5,10,15))), interval=“prediction”) # What is the differnce between “conference” and “prediction” difference?
plot(lstat,medv) abline(lm.fit) abline(lm.fit,lwd=3) abline(lm.fit,lwd=3,col=“red”) plot(lstat,medv,col=“red”) plot(lstat,medv,pch=16) plot(lstat,medv,pch=“+”) plot(1:20,1:20,pch=1:20) par(mfrow=c(2,2)) plot(lm.fit) plot(predict(lm.fit), residuals(lm.fit)) plot(predict(lm.fit), rstudent(lm.fit)) plot(hatvalues(lm.fit)) which.max(hatvalues(lm.fit))
Multiple Linear Regression
{r} lm.fit=lm(medv~lstat+age,data=Boston) summary(lm.fit) lm.fit=lm(medv~.,data=Boston) summary(lm.fit) library(car) vif(lm.fit) lm.fit1=lm(medv~.-age,data=Boston) summary(lm.fit1) lm.fit1=update(lm.fit, ~.-age)
Non-linear Transformations of the Predictors
{r} lm.fit2=lm(medv~lstat+I(lstat^2)) summary(lm.fit2) lm.fit=lm(medv~lstat) anova(lm.fit,lm.fit2) par(mfrow=c(2,2)) plot(lm.fit2) lm.fit5=lm(medv~poly(lstat,5)) summary(lm.fit5) summary(lm(medv~log(rm),data=Boston))
Qualitative Predictors
{r} # fix(Carseats) names(Carseats) lm.fit=lm(Sales~.+Income:Advertising+Price:Age,data=Carseats) summary(lm.fit) attach(Carseats) contrasts(ShelveLoc)
Interaction Terms (including interaction and single effects)
{r} summary(lm(medv~lstat*age,data=Boston))
